title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
summary: MiSTiQ replaces codebook-based vector quantizers in the KV cache with trellis-coded storage using beam search, producing reconstructions directly in MX formats such as NVFP4 so attention can run in low precision. The cost is encoding complexity (beam search per block), implementation effort for MX-Hash functions, and dependence on hardware or kernels that support MX formats for compute-side gains. It can fail if production kernels lack NVFP4 or MX support, if the compression gains do not survive on the reader's actual workload distribution, or if integration with an existing serving stack (e.g., vLLM) requires custom kernel work the team cannot maintain.
rationale: The 1.25-bit KV compression directly addresses the reader's single-24GB-GPU memory constraint and is plausibly deployable, but claimed benefits depend on MX-format kernel support and workload-specific accuracy, so it warrants a small-scale validation before adoption.
technique: Trellis-quantized KV cache with microscaling formats

claims.statement: MiSTiQ replaces codebook-based vector quantizers in the KV cache with trellis-coded storage using beam search, producing reconstructions directly in MX formats such as NVFP4 so attention can run in low precision. The cost is encoding complexity (beam search per block), implementation effort for MX-Hash functions, and dependence on hardware or kernels that support MX formats for compute-side gains. It can fail if production kernels lack NVFP4 or MX support, if the compression gains do not survive on the reader's actual workload distribution, or if integration with an existing serving stack (e.g., vLLM) requires custom kernel work the team cannot maintain.
Approximately 1.25 effective bits per KV element versus FP16, about 12.8x compression, with lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than codebook-based baselines on Llama3 and Qwen3.
